cards.title: Drew Major
cards.prompt: Move Networks' chairman came out of a networking company, not out of television. Name him and the company he came from, then say what his player did that Adobe's could not.
cards.body: Drew Major had been chief scientist at Novell, and founded Arroyo Video Systems and Edgix. The trade press drew the line in 2007: Flash streamed one constant rate through the proprietary Flash Media Server, while Move ran "at an adaptive rate off commodity components on standard HTTP servers", encoding multiple bit rates in one pass.
cards.answer: Drew Major, chairman of Move Networks, previously chief scientist at Novell. Flash pushed a single constant bit rate through Flash Media Server; Move encoded several bit rates in one pass and adapted between them off commodity components on standard HTTP servers.

cards.title: ABC ships full-length HD to a browser
cards.sub: 24 July 2007 · ABC.com beta, measured in NAB TV TechCheck
cards.prompt: A US network put full-length episodes on the web in HD and the picture held up. Give the date, say what the on-screen meter showed mid-episode, and name the thing a viewer had to install before any of it played.
cards.body: ABC launched in beta on 24 July 2007 with Desperate Housewives, Grey's Anatomy, Lost and Ugly Betty. Watched from the NAB offices, the bitrate meter under the picture read 850 kbps and peaked near 2 Mbps. The player was Move's, and Move "requires a small player applet to be downloaded to the computer".
cards.answer: 24 July 2007, in beta. The on-screen bitrate meter read 850 kbps and varied up to roughly 2 Mbps. A small Move Networks player applet had to be downloaded to the computer first.

cards.title: US Patent 7,818,444 B2
cards.sub: Brueck & Hurst · granted 19 October 2010 · provisional filed 30 April 2004
cards.prompt: One document makes the client, not the server, responsible for every bitrate switch. Name it, and say what that single choice forces the encoder to have finished before anyone presses play.
cards.body: "Apparatus, system, and method for multi-bitrate content streaming", David Brueck and Mark Hurst, assigned to Move Networks. It claims one encoded streamlet per supported bitrate per time index, each stored as "a separate content file", and "end user stations initiate each of the shifts between the different bit rates".
cards.answer: US Patent 7,818,444 B2 (Brueck and Hurst, Move Networks, granted 19 October 2010, provisional April 2004). Because the end user station initiates every shift, the encoder must already have produced a streamlet at every supported bitrate for every time index — the whole ladder, time-aligned, before the first request arrives.

cards.title: draft-pantos-http-live-streaming-00
cards.sub: R. Pantos, Apple Inc. · 1 May 2009 · Informational Internet-Draft
cards.prompt: Apple published the same architecture as an Internet-Draft two years later. Give the author and the date, then name the one thing the draft pointedly declines to specify.
cards.body: A presentation is a Playlist file, "an ordered list of additional URIs", each naming one media file. Variant Playlists let clients "switch between encodings dynamically", and every variant must carry the same content with matching sample timestamps. Then, flatly: "This document does not specify the treatment of variant streams by clients."
cards.answer: Roger Pantos of Apple, 1 May 2009. It fixes the playlist format and the variant playlist, but explicitly does not specify how a client treats variant streams — the rung-picking algorithm is left out of the standard and left in the player.

cards.title: The company goes, the shape stays
cards.prompt: Move Networks no longer exists. Say who took its assets and when, then name the three properties of its design that are still running in the player on your phone.
cards.body: EchoStar announced it had "acquired assets of Utah-based Move Networks" on 6 January 2011, six days after the transaction closed. The company went. Its shape did not: segments as immutable ordinary files any cache can serve, the whole ladder encoded before playback, and a player that picks the rung.
cards.answer: EchoStar Advanced Technologies, announced 6 January 2011 (the deal closed on 31 December 2010). What survived: immutable, cacheable segment files; the full bitrate ladder produced up front and time-aligned; and client-side rung selection. HLS is that same shape.
